sections.body_md:
BFGS stores an approximation of the inverse Hessian and updates it after every accepted step. The search direction is that approximation times the negative gradient. A line search along the direction produces a displacement \(s\) and a gradient change \(y\). The update is built from the current approximation, from \(s\), from \(y\), and from the reciprocal of the curvature product \(y^T s\).

The formula is a rank-two correction. It is arranged so that the new approximation sends \(y\) to \(s\). That is the secant equation for an inverse: if a Hessian approximation would send \(s\) to \(y\), the inverse approximation sends \(y\) back to \(s\). In one variable there is only one such number, the step divided by the gradient change, and the old approximation cancels.

Positive definiteness carries forward when two things are true. The old approximation is positive definite, and the curvature product is positive. Then the new approximation is positive definite, the next direction is a descent direction, and the formula is defined. A zero product makes the reciprocal undefined. A negative product can put a negative eigenvalue into the update. The Wolfe curvature test is what makes the product positive before the update is formed. Locally, once the approximation is faithful enough, successive error ratios tend to zero. That is superlinear convergence. It is faster than a linear rate and weaker than the squared-error bound of Newton.

sections.heading: Key equations
sections.body_md:
With \(\rho = 1/(y^T s)\) and with \(W\) the current inverse approximation,
\[
W_+ = (I - \rho s y^T)\, W\, (I - \rho y s^T) + \rho s s^T.
\]
The new matrix satisfies \(W_+ y = s\). In one variable, \(W_+ = s/y\).

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body_md:
Start from the identity, with \(s = (3,\ 0)\) and \(y = (1,\ 0)\). The curvature product is \(3\), so the reciprocal is \(1/3\). The correction that subtracts a multiple of \(s y^T\) clears the first diagonal entry, and the term built from \(s s^T\) writes \(3\) back into that entry.

The anvil entry is 3. The \((2,2)\) entry stays \(1\). The new matrix times \(y\) equals \(s\), so the inverse secant equation holds. A pair with a negative curvature product would have written a negative number in that entry, and the matrix would not have stayed positive definite.

sections.heading: Common pitfalls
sections.body_md: Using the update when the curvature product is negative, and still calling the result positive definite, contradicts the eigenvalue that the formula can introduce. A second slip is to divide by the product when it is zero. The reciprocal is undefined, so there is no update. A third is to store \(y/s\) and apply it as an inverse. That ratio approximates the Hessian. The inverse approximation is \(s/y\). A fourth is to describe the local BFGS rate as the squared-error bound. Successive ratios tending to zero are superlinear. The squared bound is the Newton claim.

sections.heading: Where this leads
sections.body_md: A conjugate-gradient iteration also avoids forming the Hessian. It builds the next direction from the gradient and a previous direction, and on a positive definite quadratic it finishes in at most as many steps as the dimension. A scaled projected step can use a positive definite matrix such as this inverse approximation as its metric. BFGS is one way to keep that matrix current. The other methods spend the same descent idea with a different memory.
